questions.prompt: What makes a decision a genuine architecture 'tradeoff,' per this course?
options: Gaining more of one desirable quality costs you some of another desirable quality, so no option maximizes everything
One option is objectively better than every alternative on every dimension that matters
The decision must involve at least two different Salesforce licenses
The decision was made without consulting any stakeholders
The decision can be reversed at no cost at any time
The decision only affects a single user's permissions
questions.explain: If one option were simply better across every quality that matters, there would be nothing to trade off -- a real tradeoff always costs you something on one axis to gain something on another.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B describes a decision that isn't actually a tradeoff at all -- if one choice dominates on every dimension, there's no real decision to make, just the obviously correct answer. A tradeoff specifically requires that no option wins on everything.

questions.prompt: A field-staff mobile app enforces MFA on every login and a 15-minute idle timeout, and users with spotty connectivity are complaining. What does this course's security-vs-usability framework say to check before loosening either control?
options: The actual sensitivity of the data being protected and how often users actually hit the control, weighed against the real cost of a breach versus the real cost of the friction
Whether the CEO personally uses the app
Whether removing MFA entirely would make the app load faster
Nothing needs to be checked -- security controls should always be loosened when users complain
questions.explain: The decision isn't security-good/usability-bad -- it's matching the control to what's actually at risk and how often the friction is felt, pricing both sides honestly rather than reflexively loosening a control because of a complaint.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: synchronous Apex is capped at 100 SOQL queries per transaction, while asynchronous Apex gets ________ SOQL queries per transaction.
questions.explain: Asynchronous Apex's higher limit (200 vs. 100) reflects that it isn't blocking a real-time interaction, which is exactly why heavy or bulk logic gets pushed to async in the first place.

questions.prompt: Match each real-time or batch Salesforce tool to its actual characteristic.
right: A custom-schema event an architect designs, useful when multiple systems need the same structured business event
A built-in feed streaming record changes automatically with no custom payload design required
An asynchronous, job-based API for processing large data volumes in the background
questions.explain: CDC is the fastest, lowest-effort real-time option since it's built in and needs no schema design. Platform Events cost more setup but buy a custom, business-meaningful payload. Bulk API 2.0 trades immediacy for the ability to safely process large volumes asynchronously.

questions.prompt: An admin's 40-element Flow has grown hard for even its author to safely trace, and the business now needs it to handle recursive, high-volume logic. What does this course's declarative-vs-programmatic reasoning say about this situation?
options: This is a signal to consider extracting the complex, high-volume piece into tested Apex called from a simplified Flow, rather than treating 'more Flow elements' as the only path forward
Flow should always be preferred regardless of volume or complexity, since it's maintainable by admins
The Flow should be deleted entirely with no replacement
Apex cannot be called from a Flow under any circumstances
questions.explain: High data volumes, recursive logic, and a point past which an admin can no longer safely trace the logic are exactly the signals this course says should push part of the solution toward Apex, often in a hybrid where Flow keeps the parts that benefit from admin visibility.

questions.prompt: Put these five parts of an Architecture Decision Record (ADR) in the order this course teaches them.
items: Context -- what problem and constraints forced this decision
Options considered -- the realistic alternatives, not just the one chosen
Decision -- which option was chosen, stated plainly
Rationale -- naming what was traded away, not just the benefit
Conditions for revisiting -- what future change would require reconsidering this
questions.explain: A good ADR moves from the forcing context, through the real alternatives considered, to a plainly stated decision, an honest rationale that names the cost, and finally the specific conditions under which the decision should be revisited.

questions.prompt: Per this course, what is the actual difference between a well-made tradeoff and an architecture mistake?
options: A well-made tradeoff has zero downside

A mistake is choosing without understanding the cost, or applying a different org's answer to your own context; a well-made tradeoff is a known cost, confirmed as acceptable, with the reasoning documented
A mistake always costs more money than a well-made tradeoff
There is no real difference between the two
questions.explain: You're not accountable for finding a zero-downside option -- none exists. You're accountable for knowing the downside, confirming the organization can live with it, and being able to explain that reasoning later.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about build-vs-buy as this course teaches it.
options: Buying usually means lower upfront cost with a recurring, headcount-scaling subscription, while building means higher upfront cost but potentially a flatter long-run cost
A managed package's hidden Apex source means subscribers can directly edit its logic whenever needed
The functional-fit test scores how much of a requirements list a package covers out of the box versus how much needs a workaround
Exit cost -- the cost of migrating away from a chosen solution later -- belongs in the original decision, not just at renewal time
Build-vs-buy is always a permanent, one-time decision that should never be revisited
questions.explain: Build vs. buy compares two cost curves, not two price tags; the functional-fit test is the practical tool for scoring a package's coverage; and exit cost is a real factor that belongs in the decision upfront. A managed package's Apex source is hidden, not directly editable, and the decision is explicitly described as revisitable as conditions change.

questions.prompt: An org buys Salesforce Shield for every user 'to be safe,' even though only 40 of 300 users handle data subject to a specific compliance requirement. What does this course's cost-vs-capability framework call this?
options: Under-provisioning
Over-provisioning -- locking in a recurring cost for capability that may sit unused by most of the org, without a concrete, current plan to use it
The only correct approach regardless of actual usage
A one-time purchase with no ongoing cost
questions.explain: Over-provisioning isn't automatically the safe choice -- it locks in ongoing per-user spend for capability the majority of users may never need, money that could fund something the org actually needs now.

questions.prompt: Using the financial-debt metaphor this course applies to speed-to-market vs. long-term design, what makes technical debt 'good debt' rather than 'bad debt'?
options: The team knows what was deferred, has a plan to pay it down, and the ongoing cost is smaller than the value of shipping on time
The shortcut was never documented or discussed with anyone
The shortcut compounds in ways nobody predicted
The team never intends to revisit the shortcut
The shortcut was taken even though the team already knew the deferred scenario was coming soon
Technical debt is always bad regardless of circumstances
questions.explain: Good debt mirrors a sound financial loan: a known, named cost, with a repayment plan, where the shortcut's value (hitting the deadline) outweighs its ongoing interest.
questions.distractorExplain: Option E describes exactly the failure mode this course calls a mistake dressed up as a shortcut -- taking the debt despite already knowing the deferred scenario is coming soon means the 'debt' was never going to be small or short-lived, which is the opposite of good debt.

questions.prompt: Match each governance model concept to what it actually does, per this course.
right: Distributes decision-making authority to individual teams, trading consistency for speed
Sorts changes by actual risk so governance intensity matches the change
Puts decision-making and change control in one place, trading speed for consistency
A hybrid where a central team owns platform-wide standards while business units retain authority within guardrails
questions.explain: Centralized design trades speed for consistency; decentralized trades consistency for speed; a Center of Excellence resolves the tension by splitting ownership; and risk tiering matches governance intensity to actual risk rather than applying one uniform process.

questions.prompt: A managed package's validation rule enforces a business rule slightly differently than an org needs, and the org cannot directly edit that rule. What does this course say is the real, specific cost being illustrated here?
options: The org has permanently traded away direct edit access to that logic for as long as the package stays installed, which is different from simply paying a subscription
The org should always choose custom code over any managed package
This cost only applies to free AppExchange packages, never paid ones
Validation rules cannot exist inside managed packages
questions.explain: This lesson's specific point is that the managed-package constraint is a technical cost distinct from the subscription price -- you've given up the ability to directly edit that hidden logic, and can only work around it, use an exposed extension point, or wait for the vendor's release cycle.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: per this course, governance is accurately described as a ________ paid on every change, in order to prevent the expensive mistakes it exists to catch.
questions.explain: Every governance step -- a review gate, a testing phase, a change advisory board -- is paid by every change that goes through it, including the overwhelming majority that were never going to be the expensive mistake governance exists to catch.

questions.prompt: A sales-ops admin starts building unsanctioned Flow automations outside the official change process because the sanctioned review queue takes six weeks for a simple list-view change. What does this course say this behavior signals?
options: That the admin is simply undisciplined and should be reprimanded, with no other action needed
A governance-design signal -- the process doesn't match the actual risk of the changes it's gating, and should prompt re-tiering the process rather than only treating this as a violation
That governance should be eliminated from the org entirely
That the admin should be given full 'Modify All' access instead
questions.explain: Shadow IT is framed as a predictable response to governance that stopped matching actual risk -- the fix is re-tiering the process (lightweight paths for low-risk changes), not only punishing the workaround.

questions.prompt: An architect opens an executive presentation with 'we chose Platform Events over Change Data Capture because we needed a custom payload schema.' Per this course's framework for explaining tradeoffs to executives, what's the problem with this opening?
options: It leads with technical mechanism instead of business impact, answering a question the executive audience didn't ask first
Platform Events are never an appropriate choice to explain to executives
The explanation is technically incorrect
Executives always prefer the most detailed technical explanation available
questions.explain: Executives are generally optimizing for cost, risk, timeline, and capability -- leading with the API name instead of business impact reads as disconnected from what the room actually asked, even when the underlying reasoning is sound.

questions.prompt: Put these four elements of this course's executive-tradeoff-explanation structure in the recommended order.
items: Business impact, stated first in terms an executive already tracks
The tradeoff, named honestly, including what's being given up
Why this is the right tradeoff for this organization specifically
What would make us revisit this decision later
questions.explain: Leading with business impact earns attention and trust; naming the honest cost lets the executive actually evaluate the choice; connecting it to this org's specific needs justifies the decision; and a named revisit trigger closes the explanation with a clear condition for reconsideration.

questions.prompt: In the Service Console case study, select every tradeoff this course identifies as present in that single scenario.
options: Performance vs. complexity (the slow-loading console)
Declarative vs. programmatic (the tangled 60-element Flow)
Governance vs. agility (how future changes to the console and logic should be reviewed)
Real-time vs. batch (a nightly financial reconciliation)
Build vs. buy (an AppExchange fleet-tracking package)
questions.explain: The Service Console case study specifically layers three tradeoffs -- performance vs. complexity, declarative vs. programmatic, and governance vs. agility -- within one scenario. Real-time vs. batch and build vs. buy are the tradeoffs featured in the separate Integration Platform case study instead.

questions.prompt: In the Integration Platform case study, why does this course treat the three data flows (live inventory, nightly order history, marketing platform sync) with three different architectures instead of one unified approach?
options: Because applying one pattern (like 'real-time, event-driven everything') to all three would pay unnecessary complexity cost on the flow that doesn't need freshness, and ignore the available shortcut for the flow that already has a vendor connector
Because Salesforce technically prevents using the same integration pattern twice in one project
Because each flow was built by a different vendor with incompatible APIs
Because real-time integration is illegal under GDPR
questions.explain: The case study's core lesson is that correctly classifying each distinct data flow against its own real requirements -- rather than picking one architecture for the whole project -- is the actual architecture skill being tested.

questions.prompt: During a practice review board challenge round, a candidate's design is shown to have a real gap. What does this course say is the stronger response?
options: Defend the original position regardless, to avoid appearing uncertain
Acknowledge the gap and revise the position, since demonstrating that update is exactly the skill a CTA review board is testing
End the presentation immediately without responding
Change the subject to an unrelated part of the design
questions.explain: A review board (and any real stakeholder challenge) is testing whether the candidate understands the tradeoffs well enough to defend or credibly revise their reasoning -- defending an indefensible position after a real gap is found is the worse outcome.

questions.prompt: Select every mistake this course's closing lesson names as a recurring tradeoff failure pattern.
options: Treating a 'best practice' as universal without checking whether this org's context matches the one that made it correct elsewhere
Choosing the more fashionable-sounding side of a tradeoff rather than the side the scenario's facts justify
Presenting a decision as costless by not naming what's being given up
Treating a tradeoff decision as permanent, with no condition named for revisiting it
Writing an Architecture Decision Record for every significant tradeoff decision
questions.explain: The closing lesson names treating best practices as universal, choosing the fashionable side, presenting a decision as costless, and treating decisions as permanent (along with misapplying a rule out of context, and solving only the first tradeoff in a compound scenario) as the recurring mistakes -- writing an ADR is the recommended practice this course teaches, not a mistake.
